items.title: Anti-Hash Survival Rig
items.statement: Build dual-hash comparator; generate collision bomb vs single weak hash locally; prove rig survives.

solutionCode.label: double polynomial hash with clock-seeded bases
solutionCode.py:
import random

M1, M2 = 1000000007, 998244353


class DoubleHash:
    """A single hash with a known (base, mod) is forgeable -- an attacker
    precomputes a Thue-Morse-style anti-hash string that collides. Two
    independent pairs seeded at runtime make that precomputation impossible."""

    def __init__(self, s: str, b1: int = None, b2: int = None):
        rng = random.Random()
        self.B1 = b1 if b1 is not None else 131 + rng.randrange(100) * 2
        self.B2 = b2 if b2 is not None else 137 + rng.randrange(100) * 2
        n = len(s)
        self.h1 = [0] * (n + 1); self.h2 = [0] * (n + 1)
        self.p1 = [1] * (n + 1); self.p2 = [1] * (n + 1)
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            c = ord(ch)
            self.h1[i+1] = (self.h1[i] * self.B1 + c) % M1
            self.h2[i+1] = (self.h2[i] * self.B2 + c) % M2
            self.p1[i+1] = self.p1[i] * self.B1 % M1
            self.p2[i+1] = self.p2[i] * self.B2 % M2

    def get(self, l: int, r: int) -> tuple:
        """Inclusive [l, r]. Compare PAIRS only, never one component."""
        a = (self.h1[r+1] - self.h1[l] * self.p1[r-l+1]) % M1
        b = (self.h2[r+1] - self.h2[l] * self.p2[r-l+1]) % M2
        return (a, b)


def weak_hash(s: str, base: int = 131, mod: int = 1000000007) -> int:
    """Single fixed hash -- the thing the rig is defending against."""
    h = 0
    for ch in s:
        h = (h * base + ord(ch)) % mod
    return h


def anti_hash_pair(k: int) -> tuple:
    """Thue-Morse construction: for base b and mod 2^64 these collide under a
    single hash. Returned here so a test can demonstrate the weakness."""
    a, b = "a", "b"
    for _ in range(k):
        a, b = a + b, b + a
    return a, b

items.complexity: O(n) to build prefix hashes, O(1) per substring comparison. Collision probability with two independent 62-bit-effective moduli is about n^2 / (M1*M2) — negligible for n up to 10^6.

followups.q: Why must the two components be compared as a pair?
followups.a: Comparing them separately and accepting either match defeats the point — you are back to a single hash. The whole strength is that a forger would have to collide under two independent moduli simultaneously, so the equality test must be on the tuple. It is a one-character mistake with a total loss of security.

followups.q: Why seed the bases at runtime rather than picking better constants?
followups.a: Any fixed constant, however exotic, can be attacked once it is known — and on a public judge your source may be visible. A base drawn from the clock differs on every execution, so no pre-built input can target it. Unpredictability, not obscurity, is what defeats the attack.

items.title: Pattern Search Triple-Threat
items.statement: Count occurrences of pattern in text three ways (KMP / Z / rolling hash); benchmark n=10⁶; report constants honestly.
hints: Hash version counts via sliding polynomial update too.

solutionCode.label: three engines that must agree on the occurrence count

items.complexity: All three are O(n + m). KMP has the smallest memory footprint; Z is the simplest to prove; rolling hash is fastest in practice but probabilistic.

followups.q: Why does the KMP counter set j = lps[j-1] after a hit instead of j = 0?
followups.a: Resetting to 0 would skip overlapping occurrences — "aaa" in "aaaa" has two, not one. Falling back to the border keeps the longest reusable prefix, so overlaps are found. Whether the problem wants overlapping matches is worth asking, because the one-character difference decides it.

On n = 10^6 all three are linear, but rolling hash usually wins on wall clock because its inner loop is two multiplies with no branching, while KMP branches on every character. Z uses the most memory (an int per position of p + s). Hash is the only probabilistic one — the verification step in the code above is what makes it exact, at the cost of an occasional O(m) compare.

items.title: Shortest Palindrome (KMP trick flagship)
items.statement: Prepend minimum chars: longest palindromic PREFIX = border of s+'#'+rev(s). Implement via lps.

solutionCode.label: longest palindromic PREFIX is the border of s + sep + reverse(s)

items.complexity: O(n) — one LPS build over a string of length 2n+1. Space O(n).

followups.a: Without it, the border can span the join and report a length longer than s itself. On s = "aa", t would be "aaaa" with a final border of 3 — nonsense, since a prefix of s cannot exceed len(s). A character that appears in neither half caps the border at len(s) and makes the answer meaningful.

followups.q: Why does the border of s + rev(s) equal the longest palindromic prefix?
followups.a: A border is a string that is both a prefix of t and a suffix of t. A prefix of t is a prefix of s; a suffix of t is a suffix of rev(s), which is a reversed prefix of s. So a border is a prefix of s that equals its own reverse — precisely a palindromic prefix, and lps gives the longest one.

items.title: Distinct Substrings Counter (bounded)
items.statement: Count distinct substrings for |s|≤1000 via O(n²) hash-set of O(1) hashes; state suffix-automaton as the O(n) future answer.

solutionCode.label: hash every substring in O(1), count the distinct pairs

items.complexity: O(n^2) substrings, each hashed in O(1) from prefix hashes — O(n^2) total. For n = 1000 that is about 500k entries, comfortably in memory.

followups.q: Why is a double hash needed rather than storing the substrings?
followups.a: Storing them costs O(n^3) memory in the worst case — 500k substrings averaging 500 characters is 250 MB. A hash pair is 16 bytes regardless of length, so the set stays around 8 MB. The trade is a vanishing collision probability for a 30x memory reduction.

followups.q: What is the real O(n) answer?
followups.a: A suffix automaton. It has at most 2n-1 states, and each state v represents len[v] - len[link[v]] distinct substrings, so summing that over all states counts them exactly in linear time with no probability involved. Worth naming even when the constraints do not require it — it signals you know this is the bounded-input shortcut.

items.title: Palindromic Range Queries
items.statement: q queries: is s[l..r] palindrome? Answer O(1) each via forward vs backward hash comparison.
hints: Backward string hashed with same rig.
Map backward indices: rev position = n−1−r … careful algebra.
Fallback center-expansion per query = O(n·q) — reject aloud.

solutionCode.label: forward hash versus reversed-string hash, with the index algebra spelled out

items.complexity: O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per query. Rejecting the O(n*q) centre-expansion fallback is the point.

followups.a: rev[k] = s[n-1-k]. The substring s[l..r] read backwards is s[r], s[r-1], ..., s[l], which in rev sits at indices n-1-r through n-1-l, in that order. Getting this off by one is the classic failure — check it on l = r = 0 with n = 1: both sides give [0,0].

Expanding around the centre of each query is O(n) per query, so O(n*q) overall — 10^10 for n and q at 10^5. The hash rig pays O(n) once and answers each query with two subtractions and a comparison. Say the number out loud rather than just calling the fallback "slower".

items.title: Repeated Substring Pattern (power trick)
items.statement: String built by tiling a piece? n − lps[n−1] divides n ⇒ yes. Prove the arithmetic.

solutionCode.label: smallest period is n minus the longest border; test divisibility

items.complexity: O(n) — one LPS build plus a divisibility test. Space O(n).

followups.q: Prove that n - lps[n-1] is the smallest period.
followups.a: A border of length b means s[0..b-1] equals s[n-b..n-1], so shifting the string by n-b lines it up with itself — that is exactly the definition of a period p = n - b. The longest border gives the smallest period. If that period divides n, the string is p repeated n/p times; if it does not divide n, the last tile is truncated and the string is not a clean repetition.

"abab": lps ends at 2, period = 4 - 2 = 2, and 4 % 2 == 0, so true — it is "ab" twice. "aba": lps ends at 1, period = 3 - 1 = 2, and 3 % 2 == 1, so false. The divisibility test is what separates a genuine tiling from a coincidental overlap, replacing an O(n * sqrt(n)) enumeration of candidate divisors.
